factCheck.evidence: Wikipedia's Filmmaking article describes filmmaking as running from an initial story idea through production to screening the finished product before an audience.
Wikipedia's Filmmaking article lists development, pre-production, production and post-production, with distribution as the final stage in which the finished film is released to audiences.
Wikipedia (Filmmaking): in development the idea is explored, rights to intellectual property may be secured, the screenplay is written and financing is obtained.
Wikipedia (Filmmaking): in pre-production all arrangements and preparations for the shoot are made, including hiring cast and crew, scouting locations and building sets.
Wikipedia (Principal photography): studio productions typically plan shooting times of about 15 to 20, 40 to 50 or, for larger productions, 80 to 100 days.
Wikipedia (Post-production): the post-production phase usually takes longer than the shooting and includes editing, color correction and the addition of music and sound.
Wikipedia (Screenplay): a screenplay is a form of narration in which the movements, actions, expressions and dialogue of characters are described for a film.
Wikipedia (Screenplay): a slug line, or master scene heading, starts each scene and says whether it is set inside or outside (INT. or EXT.), the location and the time of day.
Wikipedia (Screenplay) gives the same three parts of a slug line: interior or exterior, the specific location and the time of day.
Wikipedia (Screenplay): in studio format most screenplays transfer to the screen at about one page per minute; Final Draft's blog describes the same industry rule.
Wikipedia (Screenplay): the standard font is 12 point, 10 pitch Courier typeface.
Stephen Follows' study of screenplays describes the exacting format (12-point, 10-pitch Courier, set margins and layout) behind the one-page-one-minute industry rule.
Stephen Follows found across 2,520 scripts that a page averages about 55 seconds of screen time; Wikipedia notes the rule often bears little resemblance to the final runtime.
Wikipedia (Storyboard): a storyboard is a series of illustrations displayed in sequence to pre-visualize a motion picture; each frame lays out events as they will be seen through the camera lens.
Wikipedia (Storyboard) describes storyboards as simple illustrations or images displayed in sequence; ACMI's companion storyboarding page makes the same point that not every frame is drawn.

Wikipedia (Storyboard): storyboarding in the form widely known today was developed at the Walt Disney studio in the early 1930s, with the first complete storyboards made for the 1933 short Three Little Pigs.
Wikipedia (Storyboard): storyboards pre-visualize a film in sequence and help filmmakers plan and adjust the story before production.

SWIFF's filmmaking lesson: a shot list lists all the shots planned, is made before filming and is used during the shoot to ensure all necessary shots are captured; StudioBinder describes the same use.
SWIFF's lesson says a shot list records details such as shot type and camera movement (pan, tilt); StudioBinder lists camera movement among shot list columns.
Wikipedia (Film producer): producers select the script, arrange financing and supervise the pre-production, principal photography and post-production stages.
Wikipedia (Film director): a film director controls a film's artistic and dramatic aspects and visualizes the screenplay while guiding the cast and crew, in cooperation with the producer.
Wikipedia (Cinematographer): the cinematographer or director of photography is responsible for recording the film and is chief of the camera and lighting crews.
Wikipedia (Cinematographer): the director of photography makes artistic and technical decisions related to the image, including camera, lenses and lighting.
Wikipedia (Gaffer): the gaffer or chief lighting technician is the head electrician, responsible for executing and sometimes designing the lighting plan.
Wikipedia (Gaffer): in film and television crews the gaffer is the head electrician.
Wikipedia (Grip): grips provide camera support, especially when the camera is on a dolly or crane, work with the electrical department on lighting set-ups, and are directed by a key grip.

Wikipedia (Script supervisor): the script supervisor oversees continuity, keeps detailed notes on every take, and checks that wardrobe, props, hair and makeup match; notes help the editor cut scenes together.
Wikipedia (Continuity (fiction)): the script supervisor's job is inconspicuous because, if done well, no one may ever notice it; continuity errors can draw viewers' attention.
Wikipedia (Shot (filmmaking)) classifies shots by the camera's distance from the subject, from extreme long shots to extreme close-ups.
Wikipedia (Wide shot): a wide shot, also called a full or long shot, typically shows the entire subject with its surroundings.
Wikipedia (Medium shot): a medium shot, mid shot or waist shot is taken from a medium distance, often from the waist up.
Wikipedia (Close-up): a close-up tightly frames a person or object and is often used to show detail such as characters' emotions.
Wikipedia (Close-up): a close-up tightly frames a person or object and is often used to show detail such as characters' emotions.
Wikipedia (Medium shot) notes that references disagree: some call a full-length view a medium shot and a waist-up view a close-up, so the terms shift with context.
Wikipedia (Establishing shot): an establishing shot sets up the context for a scene and is generally a long or extreme long shot at the beginning of a scene.
Wikipedia (Establishing shot): an establishing shot sets up the context for a scene and is generally a long or extreme long shot at the beginning of a scene.
Wikipedia (Wide shot): wide shots keep the entire subject, including the full body, visible in the frame along with its surroundings.
Wikipedia (Close-up): close-ups are often used to show characters' emotions, and avoiding them can create emotional distance.
Wikipedia (Close-up): close-ups are used as cutaways to show detail such as characters' emotions.
Yale's Film Analysis guide: many films are shot with a camera at approximately the same height as its subject.
Yale's Film Analysis guide: camera angle is often used to suggest power or vulnerability; a low angle aggrandizes a figure.
Yale's Film Analysis guide: high angles can emphasize a character's dependence and smallness.
Wikipedia (The Color of Paradise): a 1999 Iranian film directed by Majid Majidi about a blind boy, Mohammad, his father Hashem and his grandmother.
ACMI's camera angles guide: the effect of low and high angles changes depending on the intent of the director or cinematographer.
Wikipedia (Dutch angle): a camera shot tilted to one side, used to portray psychological uneasiness or tension and to disorient the viewer.
Wikipedia (Dutch angle): a camera shot tilted to one side, used to portray psychological uneasiness or tension and to disorient the viewer.
Yale's Film Analysis guide describes many ways to move a camera (pans, tilts, tracking and crane shots) that change the framing during a shot.
Wikipedia (Panning (camera)): panning swivels the camera horizontally from a fixed position, and the term is derived from panorama.
Wikipedia (Panning (camera)): panning swivels the camera horizontally from a fixed position, and the term is derived from panorama.
Wikipedia (Tilt (camera)): in a tilt the camera stays in a fixed position but rotates up or down in a vertical plane.
Wikipedia (Tracking shot): the camera is often mounted on a camera dolly riding rails similar to a railroad track, and is pushed along while the scene is filmed.
Wikipedia (Tracking shot): the camera is often mounted on a camera dolly riding rails similar to a railroad track, and is pushed along while the scene is filmed.
Wikipedia (Tracking shot): dollies often ride on rails similar to a railroad track.
Wikipedia (Crane shot): a crane shot is taken by a camera on a crane or jib, moving up, down or through the air, often for wide overhead views.
Wikipedia (Dolly zoom): combining a camera move with a zoom produces a continuous perspective change, because moving the camera changes perspective while the zoom only changes the size of the view.
Wikipedia (Steadicam): the Steadicam stabilizer, invented by Garrett Brown, was introduced in 1975 to isolate the camera from the operator's movement.
Wikipedia (Normal lens): photography texts say a 50 mm lens on 35 mm approximates the angle of view of human vision; lenses shorter are wide-angle and longer are long-focus.
Wikipedia (Wide-angle lens): a wide-angle lens takes in a wider field of view and exaggerates the relative size and distance of near and far objects.
Yale's Film Analysis guide: a long (telephoto) lens compresses apparent depth so near and far elements seem at about the same distance, while a wide-angle lens exaggerates it.
Wikipedia (Perspective distortion): perspective distortion is determined by the relative distances at which an image is captured; narrow angles at long distances give a flattened image.
Wikipedia (Depth of field): depth of field is the distance between the nearest and farthest objects in acceptably sharp focus, determined by focal length, distance to subject and aperture.
Wikipedia (Depth of field): a shallow depth of field is used to isolate a subject from its background, drawing attention to it.
Wikipedia (Focus pulling): the focus puller may shift focus from one subject to another as the shot requires, a process called rack focusing.
Yale's Film Analysis guide: the intensity, direction and quality of lighting affect how an image is perceived and can focus attention on particular elements.
Wikipedia (Three-point lighting): the standard method uses a key light, a softer fill light that balances the key's shadows, and a back light that separates the subject from the background.
Wikipedia (High-key lighting): high-key lighting reduces the lighting ratio between key and fill to give a bright image with few shadows, and is often used in comedy.
Wikipedia (Low-key lighting): a high-contrast setup with a high key-to-fill ratio, commonly used in film noir, throws areas of the subject into shade.
Wikipedia (Clapperboard): the clapperboard marks scenes and takes, and its closing sticks are identified on the visual track while the clap is identified on the separate audio track.
Wikipedia (Clapperboard): the two tracks can later be precisely synchronized by matching the clap sound to the moment the sticks meet.
Wikipedia (Dogme 95): the realist Dogme 95 movement's rules banned special lighting, allowing at most a single lamp attached to the camera.
